The keys are held by leather cord and metal posts, with short bamboo pins to keep the cord from slipping out, and they are struck with wooden mallets. In the traditional music of the Ifugao in the Philippines, the gangsa is a shallow hand-held gong; the sources do not record its metal or the construction of its frame.

A full gamelan has gangsa in different registers, such as the kantilan and the pemade. It is also used in the traditional music of the Ifugao of the Cordillera in northern Luzon in the Philippines, where shallow hand-held gongs play together to accompany dance; in Bali it appears in religious ceremonies, schools, competitions and tourist settings, both as instrumental music and as dance accompaniment.

Bali's gong kebyar gamelan tradition goes back to the 1910s and later became the island's most emblematic form of sacred and secular music. A full set is usually commissioned from a workshop and normally includes nine gangsa of different sizes and registers, each with ten keys and bamboo resonators, tuned to a five-note scale over two octaves. In the second half of the twentieth century, as foreign enthusiasts bought single instruments, a one-instrument gangsa appeared. The Ifugao of the Cordillera in northern Luzon also use the same word for a shallow hand-held gong ensemble and for an individual gong; they mostly accompany dance and have no standard tuning.

甘薩琴為定音體鳴樂器，青銅或鐵製音條懸於個別竹製共鳴管上，以木槌敲擊發音。印尼甘: The gangsa is a tuned idiophone: bronze or iron bars hang over individual bamboo resonators and are struck with a wooden mallet. An Indonesian gangsa usually has ten keys over about two octaves in a five-note scale; played in pairs, two instruments are tuned slightly out of tune with each other, which produces a resonating, shimmering timbre that carries a long way. Volume and ring are controlled mainly by pressing the bar with the fingers of the free hand, and the suspended mounting lets the bar vibrate freely for longer. It is close to the older gender and saron, but the Philippine gangsa is a hand-held shallow gong ensemble with no standard pitch, its timbre varying with how the gong is held and struck.
